questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 13(1) · Meaning of a negotiable instrument
questions.stem: Section 13(1) of the Negotiable Instruments Act 1881 defines a 'negotiable instrument' as:

readLink.label: Read: What 'negotiable' means →

options.text: Any written document which is transferable by delivery
options.explanation: This is the general description drawn from the case law, not the statutory definition, and it would sweep in documents the Act never governs.

options.text: Any instrument which entitles its holder to receive money from a bank
options.explanation: A fixed deposit receipt entitles its holder to money from a bank and is not a negotiable instrument at all.

options.text: A promissory note, bill of exchange or cheque payable either to order or to bearer
options.explanation: Correct. Section 13(1) defines the term by naming the three instruments and adding the requirement that the instrument be payable to order or to bearer.

options.text: Any document of title to goods used in the ordinary course of business
options.explanation: A document of title to goods belongs to the Sale of Goods Act 1930; it is not one of the three instruments named in s. 13(1).

questions.topic: Ch 7 · Transferability and negotiability
questions.stem: The feature that distinguishes NEGOTIATION from an ordinary transfer by assignment is that:

readLink.label: Read: Transferability is not negotiability →

options.text: Negotiation requires a written instrument while an assignment may be oral
options.explanation: Both an assignment of a debt and a negotiable instrument are ordinarily in writing; writing is not what separates them.

options.text: A transferee in good faith and for value may obtain a better title than his transferor had
options.explanation: Correct. An assignee takes subject to every equity available against the assignor, whereas a holder in due course takes free from the defects in his transferor's title.

options.text: Notice must be given to the debtor in a negotiation but not in an assignment
options.explanation: This reverses the position. Notice to the debtor is a feature of an assignment; no notice is needed on a negotiation.

options.text: Consideration must be proved by a person suing on a negotiated instrument
options.explanation: Section 118(a) presumes consideration on a negotiable instrument; it is the assignee who must prove it.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · Instruments negotiable by custom
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a negotiable instrument, either under the Act or by mercantile usage?

readLink.label: Read: Negotiable by statute and by custom →

options.text: A hundi
options.explanation: A hundi is the classic instrument negotiable by mercantile usage in India and is treated as negotiable by custom.

options.text: A share warrant payable to bearer
options.explanation: A bearer share warrant passes by delivery and has long been recognised by usage as negotiable.

options.text: A bearer debenture
options.explanation: A debenture payable to bearer is transferable by delivery and is recognised as negotiable by usage.

options.text: A money order
options.explanation: Correct. A money order is a departmental instruction to pay a named person and is neither one of the three instruments in s. 13(1) nor negotiable by usage; the same is true of a postal order and a share certificate.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 118 · Presumptions
questions.stem: Which of these is NOT among the presumptions raised by section 118 of the Act?

readLink.label: Read: The presumptions the law makes →

options.text: That the instrument was duly presented for payment at maturity
options.explanation: Correct. Section 118 presumes consideration, date, time of acceptance, time of transfer, order of endorsements, the stamp on a lost instrument and holder-in-due-course status — but never due presentment, which the holder must prove or excuse under s. 76.

options.text: That every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration
options.explanation: This is s. 118(a), the first and most heavily used of the presumptions.

options.text: That every transfer of the instrument was made before its maturity
options.explanation: This is s. 118(d), which is why a defendant who says the transfer was post-maturity must prove it.

options.text: That the endorsements appearing on the instrument were made in the order in which they appear
options.explanation: This is s. 118(e), which saves a holder from having to prove the sequence of signatures.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · Proviso to s. 118(g) · Burden of proof
questions.stem: Manjari sues Devendra on a promissory note. Devendra proves that the note was obtained from its lawful owner by fraud. The effect on the burden of proof is that:

readLink.label: Read: The one presumption that flips →

options.text: Nothing changes, because the presumption that the holder is a holder in due course is conclusive
options.explanation: No presumption in s. 118 is conclusive; every limb operates only 'until the contrary is proved'.

options.text: Manjari must now prove that she is a holder in due course
options.explanation: Correct. The proviso to s. 118(g) shifts the burden onto the holder once the instrument is shown to have been obtained by an offence, by fraud or for an unlawful consideration; she must then prove consideration, good faith and acquisition before maturity.

options.text: Devendra must additionally prove that Manjari knew of the fraud
options.explanation: That would leave the burden where it began. The proviso exists precisely so the defendant need not prove the holder's state of mind.

options.text: The suit fails at once, because a note tainted by fraud is void
options.explanation: Fraud at the origin does not make the instrument void; a holder in due course may still recover on it, which is why the burden question matters.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 119 · Presumption on proof of protest
questions.stem: In a suit upon a dishonoured bill of exchange, the practical value of having had the bill protested is that:

readLink.label: Read: Presumption on proof of protest, s. 119 →

options.text: The protest converts the civil claim into a criminal one
options.explanation: Protest is an evidentiary step. Only ss. 138 to 142, and only for cheques, create criminal liability.

options.text: The protest dispenses with the need to give notice of dishonour
options.explanation: Section 102 says the opposite: where protest is required, notice OF PROTEST must be given instead of notice of dishonour, so notice is still needed.

options.text: On proof of the protest, the Court shall presume the fact of dishonour
options.explanation: Correct. Section 119 relieves the holder of proving presentment and refusal all over again, unless and until the fact of dishonour is disproved.

options.text: The protest extends the period of limitation for the suit
options.explanation: Protest has no effect on limitation; it affects only what the plaintiff must prove at the trial.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 4 · Essentials of a promissory note
questions.stem: Which of the following writings satisfies section 4 as a promissory note?

readLink.label: Read: Promissory note, s. 4 →

options.text: 'I promise to pay Harini ₹ 90,000 as soon as my consignment from Tuticorin is sold.' Signed.
options.explanation: The promise depends on an event that may never happen, so it is conditional and fails the requirement of an unconditional undertaking.

options.text: 'I acknowledge myself to be indebted to Harini in the sum of ₹ 90,000.' Signed.
options.explanation: An acknowledgement of debt is not a promise to pay; s. 4 requires an undertaking, not a mere admission.

options.text: 'I promise to pay Harini ₹ 90,000 and to deliver 200 metres of cloth.' Signed.
options.explanation: The sum must be money only. Adding an obligation to deliver goods destroys the certainty s. 4 requires.

options.text: 'I promise to pay Harini or order ₹ 90,000 on 31 December 2026.' Signed.
options.explanation: Correct. The undertaking is unconditional — a stated future date is certain to arrive and is not a condition — the sum is certain and in money only, and the parties are certain.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 4 · Currency notes excluded
questions.stem: A currency note issued by the Reserve Bank of India is not a promissory note because:

readLink.label: Read: Promissory note, s. 4 →

options.text: Section 4 expressly excludes a bank note and a currency note from the definition
options.explanation: Correct. The definition opens by carving out bank notes and currency notes, which is why the note in your pocket is money and not paper governed by this Act.

options.text: It is not signed by the person who promises to pay
options.explanation: A currency note does carry the Governor's signature; the exclusion does not rest on the absence of a signature.

options.text: It is payable to bearer rather than to order
options.explanation: Instruments payable to bearer are expressly within s. 13(1); being a bearer instrument is no disqualification.

options.text: It carries no stamp under the Indian Stamp Act
options.explanation: Absence of a stamp affects enforceability of an ordinary note, but the reason a currency note is outside s. 4 is the express exclusion in the section itself.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 5 · Bill of exchange
questions.stem: The essential feature that makes an instrument a bill of exchange under section 5 rather than a promissory note under section 4 is that it contains:

readLink.label: Read: Bill of exchange, s. 5 →

options.text: A promise by the debtor to pay on a fixed date
options.explanation: A promise by the debtor is the hallmark of a promissory note, not a bill.

options.text: An unconditional order directing a certain person to pay a certain sum of money
options.explanation: Correct. Section 5 replaces the note's 'undertaking' with an 'order', and it is that order, given by the creditor to a third person, that brings in the drawee and makes acceptance necessary.

options.text: A direction to a banker and nobody else
options.explanation: A direction confined to a banker, payable on demand, would make it a cheque under s. 6. A bill may be drawn on any person.

options.text: A conditional order which becomes absolute on acceptance
options.explanation: The order must be unconditional when the bill is drawn; acceptance does not cure a condition written into the order.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 6 · Cheque and truncated cheque
questions.stem: Under section 6, a 'truncated cheque' means a cheque:

readLink.label: Read: Cheque, s. 6 →

options.text: Drawn for an amount smaller than the balance standing to the drawer's credit
options.explanation: Truncation has nothing to do with the amount or the balance; it is about how the cheque physically travels.

options.text: Drawn in electronic form using a secure system with a digital signature
options.explanation: That describes the other limb of s. 6 — a cheque in the electronic form — which is a different creature from a truncated cheque.

options.text: Truncated during the course of a clearing cycle, its physical movement being stopped and replaced by an electronic image
options.explanation: Correct. Truncation stops the paper cheque moving further and substitutes an electronic image for the rest of the clearing cycle, either by the clearing house or by the paying or receiving bank.

options.text: Whose validity period has expired, so that the banker returns it as outdated
options.explanation: A cheque more than three months old is a stale cheque, which is a matter of banking practice and not the s. 6 definition.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 4, 5, 6 · The three instruments compared
questions.stem: Which statement about a cheque is correct?

readLink.label: Read: The three instruments compared →

options.text: A cheque must be accepted by the banker before the drawer becomes liable on it
options.explanation: A cheque needs no acceptance at all. The drawer is liable from the moment the cheque is issued.

options.text: A cheque is entitled to three days of grace like any other bill of exchange
options.explanation: Section 22 gives grace only to instruments NOT payable on demand. A cheque is payable on demand, so it gets no grace.

options.text: A cheque must be stamped under the Indian Stamp Act to be valid
options.explanation: Notes and bills require a stamp; a cheque does not, which is one of the standard rows in the comparison table.

options.text: A cheque may be crossed, whereas a promissory note and a bill of exchange may not
options.explanation: Correct. Sections 123 to 131A apply to cheques alone; crossing has no meaning on a note or on an ordinary bill.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 7 · Drawee in case of need
questions.stem: A bill drawn by Suhasini on Tarun names Umesh as the person to be resorted to in case of need. When Tarun refuses to accept the bill, the correct position is that:

readLink.label: Read: Drawee in case of need →

options.text: The bill is not treated as dishonoured until it has also been presented to Umesh and he too has refused
options.explanation: Correct. A drawee in case of need is named by the drawer on the face of the bill precisely as a fall-back, and the holder must resort to him before treating the bill as dishonoured.

options.text: The bill is dishonoured at once, and Umesh has no role unless he volunteers to accept for honour
options.explanation: That confuses the drawee in case of need with an acceptor for honour, who appears only after a noting or protest.

options.text: Umesh becomes primarily liable on the bill from the moment it is drawn
options.explanation: Naming a person in case of need creates no liability in him until he accepts; the acceptor alone is primarily liable.

options.text: Suhasini must first protest the bill before Umesh can be approached
options.explanation: Protest precedes an acceptance for honour, not a resort to the drawee in case of need, whose name already appears on the bill.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 108, 113 · Acceptance and payment for honour
questions.stem: The difference between an acceptor for honour and a person who pays a bill for honour is that:

readLink.label: Read: Acceptor for honour and payment for honour →

options.text: Only the acceptor for honour needs the consent of the holder; the payer for honour needs the consent of the drawer
options.explanation: The consent point is right for the acceptor but wrong for the payer: a payer for honour needs no consent from the drawer, only a declaration before a notary.

options.text: Acceptance for honour follows a noting or protest for non-acceptance, while payment for honour follows a protest for non-payment
options.explanation: Correct. The two rescue steps sit at different points on the timeline: one after the bill has been protested or noted for non-acceptance, the other after it has been protested for non-payment.

options.text: An acceptor for honour must already be liable on the bill, while a payer for honour must not be
options.explanation: This reverses s. 108, which requires the acceptor for honour to be a person NOT already liable on the bill.

options.text: Only the payer for honour acquires rights against prior parties
options.explanation: Both acquire rights: the acceptor for honour who pays, and the payer for honour, each step into the shoes of the holder against the party for whose honour he acted.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 8 · Holder
questions.stem: Ganesh's clerk carries a bearer cheque to the bank to encash it for his employer. Nirmala steals a bearer cheque and holds it. Which of them is a 'holder' within section 8?

readLink.label: Read: Holder, s. 8 →

options.text: Both, because each is in possession of the instrument
options.explanation: Possession alone is not enough. Section 8 needs entitlement in one's own name as well.

options.text: The clerk only, because he holds it with his employer's authority
options.explanation: Authority to collect is not entitlement in his own name; the clerk holds for Ganesh and the right is Ganesh's.

options.text: Neither, because neither is entitled in his or her own name to possession and to recover the amount
options.explanation: Correct. The clerk holds for his employer and so is not entitled in his own name; the thief has possession but no entitlement at all. Section 8 requires both limbs.

options.text: Nirmala only, because a bearer instrument passes to whoever holds it
options.explanation: A bearer instrument passes by delivery made for the purpose of negotiation. Theft is not such a delivery, so no title passes.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 9 · Holder in due course
questions.stem: Vasanthi receives a bill as a birthday gift from her uncle three days before it matures. She knows of no defect in his title. She is:

readLink.label: Read: Holder in due course, s. 9 →

options.text: A holder in due course, because she took the bill before maturity and in good faith
options.explanation: Two of the three conditions are met but the third is missing; s. 9 also requires consideration.

options.text: A holder in due course, because good faith is the only test the section applies
options.explanation: Good faith is one limb of s. 9, not the whole of it. Consideration and acquisition before maturity are equally necessary.

options.text: Neither a holder nor a holder in due course, because a donee acquires nothing
options.explanation: A donee who is entitled in her own name to possession and to recover the amount is a holder under s. 8; the gift does not deprive her of that status.

options.text: A holder but not a holder in due course, because she gave no consideration
options.explanation: Correct. Section 9 requires the person to have become the possessor or endorsee FOR CONSIDERATION, so a donee is always a holder and never a holder in due course.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 10 · Payment in due course
questions.stem: A banker pays a bill of exchange to the holder two weeks BEFORE its maturity, in good faith and without negligence. The payment is:

readLink.label: Read: Payment in due course, s. 10 →

options.text: Not a payment in due course, because it was not made in accordance with the apparent tenor of the instrument
options.explanation: Correct. The first limb of s. 10 requires payment according to the apparent tenor, and a time instrument is not payable until maturity; good faith cannot cure a payment made too early.

options.text: A payment in due course, because good faith and absence of negligence are the only requirements
options.explanation: Those are two of the four limbs. Section 10 also requires the payment to follow the apparent tenor and to be made to the person in possession.

options.text: A payment in due course, because early payment can never prejudice the holder
options.explanation: Whether the holder is prejudiced is beside the point; s. 10 sets objective conditions and the tenor condition fails.

options.text: Not a payment in due course, because payment to a holder never discharges an instrument
options.explanation: Section 78 requires payment to be made to the holder; paying the holder is right, and it is the timing that is wrong here.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 20 · Inchoate stamped instrument
questions.stem: Prabhu signs and delivers to Rekha a stamped paper, blank as to the amount, authorising her to fill it in for not more than ₹ 50,000. Rekha fills in ₹ 2,00,000, an amount within the stamp, and negotiates the note to Sridhar, who takes it for value in good faith before maturity. Prabhu's liability is:

readLink.label: Read: Inchoate stamped instrument, s. 20 →

options.text: ₹ 50,000 to Sridhar and ₹ 50,000 to Rekha, the authorised amount in each case
options.explanation: The private limit binds only the immediate party. A holder in due course is not confined to it, so Sridhar recovers more than ₹ 50,000.

options.text: ₹ 2,00,000 to Sridhar, but only ₹ 50,000 had Rekha herself sued
options.explanation: Correct. Section 20 makes the signer liable to a HOLDER IN DUE COURSE for the whole amount filled in, so long as it is within the stamp, while the proviso confines any other person to the amount the signer intended to be paid.

options.text: Nothing at all, because he never wrote the amount himself
options.explanation: Signing and delivering a blank stamped paper is precisely what s. 20 treats as prima facie authority to complete the instrument.

options.text: ₹ 2,00,000 to anyone who holds the note, whether or not he gave value
options.explanation: The full amount is recoverable only by a holder in due course; a holder who gave no value falls under the proviso and is limited to ₹ 50,000.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 53 · Title derived from a holder in due course
questions.stem: A obtains a bill from B by fraud and endorses it to C, who takes it for value, in good faith and before maturity. C endorses it to D, who knows all about the fraud. D sues B. D will:

readLink.label: Read: The privileges of a holder in due course →

options.text: Fail, because a person with notice of a fraud can never enforce the instrument
options.explanation: That would be true of a transferee from a defective title, but D derives his title from C, whose title was clean.

options.text: Fail, unless he can prove that he himself gave consideration
options.explanation: Consideration would make D a holder for value but would not answer the fraud. What saves him is the source of his title, not his own payment.

options.text: Succeed, because a holder who derives title from a holder in due course has the rights of that holder in due course
options.explanation: Correct. Section 53 cleanses the instrument once it has passed through the hands of a holder in due course, and every later holder takes the cleansed title unless he was himself a party to the original fraud.

options.text: Succeed, because s. 118(g) conclusively presumes every holder to be a holder in due course
options.explanation: The presumption in s. 118(g) is rebuttable, and here it is displaced by D's admitted knowledge. Section 53, not the presumption, is what wins the case.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 43 · Instrument without consideration
questions.stem: Section 43 provides that an instrument made or accepted without consideration:

readLink.label: Read: Want of consideration, s. 43 →

options.text: Is void from the beginning and cannot be enforced by anyone
options.explanation: The instrument is not void. It simply creates no obligation between the parties to that transaction.

options.text: May be enforced by any person into whose hands it later comes, with or without value
options.explanation: Section 43 protects a holder who took FOR CONSIDERATION, and those deriving title from him — not every later possessor.

options.text: Can be enforced only after the party who signed it ratifies the transaction in writing
options.explanation: No ratification requirement appears anywhere in the section; the protection turns on the holder having given consideration.

options.text: Creates no obligation between the parties to that transaction, but a holder who takes it for consideration, and every subsequent holder deriving title from him, may recover from any prior party
options.explanation: Correct. Want of consideration is a complete defence between the immediate parties and no defence at all once the instrument reaches a holder who gave value.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 120 to 122 · Estoppels
questions.stem: In a suit by a subsequent holder, an ENDORSER of a negotiable instrument is not permitted to deny:

readLink.label: Read: Estoppels, ss. 120 to 122 →

options.text: The signature or capacity to contract of any prior party to the instrument
options.explanation: Correct. That is exactly the estoppel s. 122 creates against an endorser, and it is what makes a chain of endorsements commercially reliable.

options.text: The validity of the instrument as originally made or drawn
options.explanation: That estoppel binds the maker, the drawer and an acceptor for the honour of the drawer under s. 120, not the endorser.

options.text: The capacity of the payee to endorse at the date of the instrument
options.explanation: That estoppel is in s. 121 and binds the maker of a note and the acceptor of a bill payable to order.

options.text: That the instrument was duly presented for payment at maturity
options.explanation: No section estops an endorser on presentment; on the contrary, s. 35 makes his liability conditional on due notice of dishonour.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 11, 12 · Inland and foreign instruments
questions.stem: A bill is drawn in Jaipur upon Deepak, who is resident in Jaipur, and is made payable in Dubai. The bill is:

readLink.label: Read: Inland and foreign instruments →

options.text: A foreign instrument, because it is payable outside India
options.explanation: Being payable abroad is not decisive. Section 11 offers two alternative limbs and this bill satisfies the second.

options.text: An inland instrument, because it is drawn in India upon a person resident in India
options.explanation: Correct. Section 11 makes an instrument inland if it is drawn or made in India AND EITHER made payable in India OR drawn upon a person resident in India; the second limb is satisfied here.

options.text: A foreign instrument, and it must therefore be protested on dishonour in every case
options.explanation: The classification is wrong, and even for a genuine foreign bill s. 104 requires protest only where the law of the place of drawing requires it.

options.text: Neither, because an instrument payable in two countries falls outside the Act
options.explanation: The Act has no such category. Every instrument is either inland under s. 11 or foreign under s. 12.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 17 · Ambiguous instrument
questions.stem: Bhavana draws a bill on herself, so that the drawer and the drawee are the same person. Under section 17 the holder may:

readLink.label: Read: Ambiguous instrument, s. 17 →

options.text: Do nothing, because such an instrument is void for uncertainty
options.explanation: Section 17 exists precisely to save such instruments; nothing about them is void.

options.text: Require Bhavana to redraw the instrument in a proper form
options.explanation: The section gives the holder an election, not a right to demand a fresh instrument.

options.text: At his election treat it either as a bill of exchange or as a promissory note, and it is thenceforward treated accordingly
options.explanation: Correct. Where an instrument may be construed either way, s. 17 gives the choice to the holder, and the election once made fixes the character of the instrument.

options.text: Treat it only as a promissory note, the drawee being incapable of accepting his own order
options.explanation: Treating it as a note is one of the two options, but the section leaves the choice with the holder rather than compelling it.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 18 · Figures and words differing
questions.stem: A promissory note states the sum as '₹ 65,000' in figures and as 'Rupees fifty-six thousand only' in words. The sum undertaken to be paid is:

readLink.label: Read: Figures and words, s. 18 →

options.text: ₹ 65,000, the larger of the two sums
options.explanation: The Act contains no rule preferring the larger sum; it prefers the words whichever way the difference runs.

options.text: ₹ 65,000, because figures are the more precise expression
options.explanation: Section 18 takes the opposite view, on the footing that words are harder to alter than figures.

options.text: Nothing, because the note is void for uncertainty of the sum
options.explanation: Section 18 supplies the answer, so there is no uncertainty left to make the note void.

options.text: ₹ 56,000, the amount stated in words
options.explanation: Correct. Section 18 provides that where the amount is stated differently in figures and in words, the amount stated in WORDS is the amount undertaken or ordered to be paid.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 13(2) · Payable to order
questions.stem: A cheque is drawn 'Pay Ravi'. The words 'or order' do not appear anywhere on it and nothing else is written. The cheque is:

readLink.label: Read: Payable to order and to bearer, s. 13(2) →

options.text: Payable to order, since it contains no words prohibiting transfer or indicating that it shall not be transferable
options.explanation: Correct. Section 13(2) asks only whether words PROHIBITING transfer are present; the mere absence of 'or order' does not restrict the instrument.

options.text: Not negotiable, because the words 'or order' are an essential part of every negotiable instrument
options.explanation: The words are usual but not essential. What matters is whether transfer has been prohibited.

options.text: Payable to bearer, because no method of transfer has been specified
options.explanation: An instrument is payable to bearer only where it is expressed to be so, or where the only or last endorsement is in blank.

options.text: Void, because the drawer has failed to state whether it is an order or a bearer instrument
options.explanation: Section 13(2) supplies the classification in exactly this situation, so nothing is left uncertain.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 42 · Bill drawn in a fictitious name
questions.stem: The acceptor of a bill drawn in a fictitious name and payable to the drawer's order is liable to a holder in due course provided the holder can show that:

readLink.label: Read: Fictitious instruments, s. 42 →

options.text: The acceptor knew that the drawer's name was fictitious when he accepted
options.explanation: The section does not turn on the acceptor's knowledge; it fixes him with liability whether or not he knew.

options.text: The first endorsement on the bill and the drawer's signature are in the same handwriting
options.explanation: Correct. That single evidentiary condition is what s. 42 requires, and it establishes that the bill came from the same hand that the acceptor dealt with.

options.text: The bill was protested for non-acceptance before it was negotiated
options.explanation: Protest belongs to ss. 99 to 104 and has nothing to do with the s. 42 condition.

options.text: He himself took the bill directly from the fictitious drawer
options.explanation: The section protects a holder in due course however far down the chain he sits; direct dealing is not required.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 46, 47 · Delivery
questions.stem: Sarita hands her friend a bearer cheque and asks him to keep it in his safe until she returns from Chennai. The friend later claims to be the holder. The correct position is:

readLink.label: Read: Negotiation and delivery, ss. 46 and 47 →

options.text: The cheque was negotiated to him, because a bearer instrument passes by delivery alone
options.explanation: Delivery alone is not enough. Section 47 requires the delivery to have been made FOR THE PURPOSE OF NEGOTIATION.

options.text: The cheque was negotiated to him unless Sarita proves fraud on his part
options.explanation: No question of fraud arises. The purpose of the delivery decides the matter, and safe custody is not negotiation.

options.text: The cheque was not negotiated, because the delivery was for safe custody and not for the purpose of negotiation
options.explanation: Correct. Section 47 negotiates a bearer instrument only where the delivery is made for the purpose of negotiation; s. 46 adds that as between immediate parties a delivery may be shown to have been for a special purpose only.

options.text: The cheque was negotiated, but Sarita may recall it at any time before it is presented
options.explanation: There is no right to recall a negotiated instrument. The correct analysis is that no negotiation took place at all.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 49 · Blank endorsement made full
questions.stem: Under section 49, the holder of an instrument endorsed in blank may convert the blank endorsement into an endorsement in full. The consequence of doing so is that:

readLink.label: Read: Converting a blank endorsement, s. 49 →

options.text: He becomes liable as an endorser to every subsequent holder
options.explanation: He writes the direction ABOVE the earlier signature without signing himself, so he never becomes an endorser and never incurs an endorser's liability.

options.text: The instrument ceases to be negotiable in the hands of the new endorsee
options.explanation: A full endorsement keeps the instrument payable to order and fully negotiable; only a restrictive endorsement stops further negotiation.

options.text: The original blank endorsement is treated as cancelled and the earlier endorser is discharged
options.explanation: Nothing is cancelled. The earlier endorser remains liable on his own signature exactly as before.

options.text: The instrument becomes payable to the named endorsee and can pass only on that person's endorsement, while the converting holder incurs no endorser's liability
options.explanation: Correct. Section 49 lets a holder protect himself by naming the next taker without signing his own name, so he gains the protection of a full endorsement without taking on the liability of an endorser.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 51 · Who may negotiate
questions.stem: Under section 51, a payee or an endorsee of a negotiable instrument may endorse and negotiate it only if:

readLink.label: Read: Who may negotiate, s. 51 →

options.text: He is the holder of the instrument, and its negotiability has not been restricted or excluded
options.explanation: Correct. Section 51 opens the right to every sole maker, drawer, payee or endorsee where negotiability is intact, and its proviso adds that a payee or endorsee cannot endorse unless he is the holder.

options.text: He has given value for the instrument
options.explanation: Consideration matters to holder-in-due-course status under s. 9, not to the power to negotiate under s. 51.

options.text: The maker or drawer has consented in writing to the transfer
options.explanation: No consent is needed. Free transferability without reference to the debtor is the essence of negotiability.

options.text: The instrument has not yet been accepted
options.explanation: Acceptance is irrelevant to the power to negotiate; an accepted bill is negotiated every day.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 56 · Partial endorsement and part payment
questions.stem: Yashwant holds a promissory note for ₹ 8,00,000 made by Zubin. Zubin pays ₹ 3,00,000 against it and a note of that part payment is endorsed on the instrument. The amount for which the instrument may lawfully be negotiated thereafter is:

readLink.label: Read: Endorsement for part of the amount, s. 56 →

options.explanation: This ignores the part payment. Once ₹ 3,00,000 has been paid, only the residue remains due on the instrument.

Correct. Section 56 forbids a writing that transfers only part of the amount appearing to be due, but where the amount has been PARTLY PAID a note of that fact may be endorsed and the instrument negotiated for the residue: ₹ 8,00,000 − ₹ 3,00,000 = ₹ 5,00,000.
This is the sum already paid, which is the one amount that can no longer be negotiated at all.

options.text: Nothing, because any endorsement after a part payment is invalid
options.explanation: The second half of s. 56 exists precisely to permit negotiation of the residue after a noted part payment.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 59, 60 · Negotiation after maturity
questions.stem: Naveen takes an endorsement of a bill four days AFTER it has matured and been dishonoured, knowing of the dishonour. His position is that:

readLink.label: Read: Negotiation before and after maturity, s. 60 →

options.text: The endorsement is void, since an instrument cannot be negotiated after maturity
options.explanation: Section 60 allows negotiation until payment or satisfaction at or after maturity, so the endorsement is perfectly valid.

options.text: He becomes a holder in due course, because he gave value and acted honestly
options.explanation: Section 9 requires acquisition BEFORE the amount became payable, which he cannot satisfy.

options.text: He is a valid holder, but has only the rights his transferor had against the other parties
options.explanation: Correct. Section 60 keeps the instrument negotiable until payment or satisfaction, while s. 59 confines a person taking after dishonour or maturity to the rights of his transferor.

options.text: He may recover from the acceptor but from nobody else
options.explanation: His remedies are limited by his transferor's rights, not by an artificial rule confining him to the acceptor.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 50 · Restrictive endorsement
questions.stem: An endorsement reading 'Pay Kiran for collection' has the effect that:

readLink.label: Read: The kinds of endorsement →

options.text: The endorser excludes his own liability on the instrument
options.explanation: That is the effect of a sans recours endorsement under s. 52, which uses quite different words.

options.text: The instrument becomes payable to bearer in Kiran's hands
options.explanation: Only a blank endorsement has that effect. This endorsement names a person and adds a restriction.

options.text: The endorsement is invalid because it attaches a purpose to the transfer
options.explanation: Section 50 expressly permits an endorsement that constitutes the endorsee an agent to receive the contents, so nothing is invalid.

options.text: Kiran may receive payment but cannot negotiate the instrument further
options.explanation: Correct. Section 50 lets an endorsement restrict or exclude the right of further negotiation, or make the endorsee a mere agent to receive the contents for the endorser.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 52 · Sans recours endorsement
questions.stem: Lakshmi endorses a bill 'Pay Mohan or order, sans recours'. The bill is later negotiated through three further endorsers and comes back to Lakshmi as holder. On dishonour, Lakshmi may:

readLink.label: Read: Sans recours endorsement, s. 52 →

options.text: Sue all the intermediate endorsers, because she had excluded her own liability to them
options.explanation: Correct. The rule against negotiation back would normally stop a prior party suing intermediate parties, but s. 52 says expressly that an endorser who excluded his liability and later becomes the holder may hold every intermediate endorser liable to him.

options.text: Sue nobody, because a prior party who becomes the holder again may never sue intermediate parties
options.explanation: That is the general rule on negotiation back, but s. 52 creates the express exception this question is testing.

options.text: Sue only Mohan, her immediate endorsee
options.explanation: There is no rule confining her to her immediate endorsee; s. 52 opens the whole intermediate chain to her.

options.text: Sue the intermediate endorsers only if she first pays the bill herself
options.explanation: She has excluded her own liability, so there is nothing for her to pay before suing.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 123, 124 · General and special crossing
questions.stem: Which statement about the crossing of cheques is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Crossing of cheques →

options.text: Two parallel transverse lines are essential to a special crossing
options.explanation: They are essential to a GENERAL crossing under s. 123. For a special crossing under s. 124 the name of a banker is what matters, and the lines are optional.

options.text: A holder may convert a general crossing into a special crossing, but not the other way round
options.explanation: Correct. Section 125 permits a crossing to be made more restrictive at each step — uncrossed to crossed, general to special, and the addition of 'not negotiable' — and never less restrictive.

options.text: Only the drawer may cross a cheque, and only at the time of drawing it
options.explanation: Section 125 lets the HOLDER cross an uncrossed cheque, and a crossing may be added after issue.

options.text: A promissory note may be crossed in the same way as a cheque
options.explanation: Crossing applies to cheques alone. Sections 123 to 131A have no application to notes or ordinary bills.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 130 · Not negotiable crossing
questions.stem: A cheque is crossed generally with the words 'not negotiable'. The effect of those words is that the cheque:

readLink.label: Read: The 'not negotiable' crossing, s. 130 →

options.text: Cannot be transferred at all, and any transfer is a nullity
options.explanation: The cheque remains freely transferable. Only words such as 'Pay X only' written on the face destroy transferability.

options.text: Can be paid only into the account of the named payee
options.explanation: That is the practical effect of an 'account payee' crossing, which is banking practice and not s. 130.

options.text: Remains transferable, but a transferee cannot get, and cannot give, a better title than the person from whom he took it had
options.explanation: Correct. Section 130 leaves transferability intact and removes only negotiability — the capacity of a transfer to cure a defect in title, which is why an innocent taker from a thief recovers nothing.

options.text: Must be refused payment by the drawee banker
options.explanation: Refusal is required only under s. 127, where a cheque is crossed specially to more than one banker.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 131 · Account payee crossing
questions.stem: An 'account payee' crossing on a cheque:

readLink.label: Read: Account payee and the collecting banker →

options.text: Is defined in s. 124 as a third kind of statutory crossing
options.explanation: Section 124 defines a special crossing by the name of a banker. No section of the Act defines an account payee crossing.

options.text: Binds the paying banker, who must refuse payment of such a cheque
options.explanation: The paying banker's duties come from ss. 126 and 129 and concern general and special crossings. An account payee crossing is not aimed at him.

options.text: Makes the cheque non-transferable in law
options.explanation: It does not. It is a direction about where the proceeds go, not a restriction written into the instrument's transferability.

options.text: Is not defined in the Act at all, and operates in practice as a direction to the collecting banker, whose disregard of it is ordinarily negligence under s. 131
options.explanation: Correct. It is a creature of banking practice, and its force comes from the fact that a collecting banker who ignores it loses the s. 131 protection because he cannot show he acted without negligence.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 127 · Double special crossing
questions.stem: A cheque bears the names of two different bankers across its face, and the second is not named as an agent for collection. The drawee banker must:

readLink.label: Read: A cheque crossed specially more than once, s. 127 →

options.text: Refuse payment of the cheque
options.explanation: Correct. Section 127 requires the drawee banker to refuse payment where a cheque is crossed specially to more than one banker, except where the second crossing is to an agent for the purpose of collection.

options.text: Pay the banker whose name was written first
options.explanation: The section gives no priority to the first name; it directs an outright refusal.

options.text: Pay either banker, at his own choice
options.explanation: A choice would defeat the purpose of a special crossing, which is to fix a single route for the money.

options.text: Treat the cheque as crossed generally and pay any banker
options.explanation: A special crossing cannot be downgraded to a general one; s. 125 allows a crossing to be made only more restrictive.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 22, 23 · Maturity of a bill payable months after date
questions.stem: A bill of exchange is dated 30 November 2026 and is payable three months after date. No public holiday falls on or near the resulting date. The due date of the bill is:

readLink.label: Read: Maturity, days of grace and the due date →

options.text: 28 February 2027
options.explanation: This is only the day the bill is EXPRESSED to be payable under s. 23. The three days of grace in s. 22 have been forgotten.

options.text: 3 March 2027
options.explanation: Correct. February 2027 has no 30th, so s. 23 sends the period to the last day of that month, 28 February 2027; s. 22 then puts the bill at maturity on the third day after, that is 3 March 2027.

options.text: 2 March 2027
options.explanation: This counts the day the bill is expressed to be payable as the first of the three days of grace. Section 22 makes the instrument mature on the third day AFTER that day.

options.text: 5 March 2027
options.explanation: This reads s. 23 as rolling a missing 30 February forward into March. The section does the opposite: where there is no corresponding day, the period ends on the LAST DAY of that month.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 22, 24 · Maturity of a bill payable days after date
questions.stem: A bill of exchange is dated 3 August 2026 and is payable 100 days after date. No public holiday falls on or near the resulting date. The due date of the bill is:

readLink.label: Read: Days, s. 24, and the days of grace →

options.text: 11 November 2026
options.explanation: This is the day the bill is expressed to be payable once s. 24 has been applied correctly, but it omits the three days of grace required by s. 22.

options.text: 13 November 2026
options.explanation: This counts 3 August itself as the first of the 100 days. Section 24 requires the day of the date to be EXCLUDED, so the count starts on 4 August.

options.text: 14 November 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Excluding 3 August, the 100th day is 11 November 2026 (28 days in August, 30 in September, 31 in October and 11 in November); adding the three days of grace gives 14 November 2026, a Saturday, which is an ordinary business day.

options.text: No due date can be fixed, because s. 24 applies only to bills payable after sight
options.explanation: Section 24 applies to an instrument payable a stated number of days after date, after sight OR after a certain event, so it governs this bill directly.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 21, 22, 23 · Bill payable after sight
questions.stem: A bill of exchange is dated 5 January 2026 and is payable two months after sight. The drawee accepts it on 10 January 2026. No public holiday falls on or near the resulting date. The due date of the bill is:

readLink.label: Read: 'After sight', s. 21 →

options.text: 5 March 2026
options.explanation: This runs the two months from the date of the bill and then forgets the days of grace as well — two errors in one figure.

options.text: 8 March 2026
options.explanation: This is the classic after-sight trap: two months counted from the DATE OF THE BILL plus three days of grace. On a bill, s. 21 makes 'after sight' run from ACCEPTANCE.

options.text: 10 March 2026
options.explanation: The starting point is right — two months from acceptance on 10 January — but the three days of grace under s. 22 have been left out.

options.text: 13 March 2026
options.explanation: Correct. On a bill, 'after sight' runs from acceptance (s. 21), so the two months run from 10 January 2026 to 10 March 2026 (s. 23); adding the three days of grace under s. 22 gives 13 March 2026.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 22, 23, 25 · Maturity falling on a public holiday
questions.stem: A bill of exchange is dated 29 June 2026 and is payable three months after date. 2 October is a notified public holiday and no other holiday falls in the period. The due date of the bill is:

readLink.label: Read: Maturity on a public holiday, s. 25 →

options.text: 1 October 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Three months from 29 June 2026 is 29 September 2026 (s. 23); adding three days of grace gives 2 October 2026 (s. 22), which is a public holiday, so s. 25 makes the instrument due on the next PRECEDING business day, 1 October 2026.

options.text: 3 October 2026
options.explanation: This moves the maturity forward. Section 25 moves it BACK to the next preceding business day; only the practice for an emergency holiday moves payment forward.

options.text: 2 October 2026
options.explanation: This is the date the days of grace produce, but s. 25 does not allow an instrument to mature on a public holiday.

options.text: 29 September 2026
options.explanation: This is the day the bill is expressed to be payable, with the three days of grace omitted altogether.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 79 · Interest where a rate is specified
questions.stem: A promissory note for ₹ 6,00,000 is dated 1 June 2026, is payable twelve months after date, and bears on its face the words 'with interest at 12 per cent per annum'. The maker pays the note on 1 September 2027, exactly fifteen months after the date of the instrument. The interest recoverable under section 79 is:

readLink.label: Read: Interest, ss. 79 and 80 →

options.explanation: This runs the specified rate over the twelve-month tenor only. Section 79 runs interest from the date of the instrument until tender or realisation, which is fifteen months here.
Correct. Section 79 applies the SPECIFIED rate from the DATE OF THE INSTRUMENT until realisation: ₹ 6,00,000 × 12% × 15/12 = ₹ 90,000.
This applies the 18 per cent rate in s. 80. That rate operates only where the instrument specifies NO rate; here a rate is expressly stated.
This runs interest only for the three months after maturity, which is the s. 80 starting point, not the s. 79 one.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 80 · Interest where no rate is specified
questions.stem: A promissory note for ₹ 4,50,000 says nothing about interest. It fell due on 10 April 2026 and the maker pays it exactly eight months later. The interest recoverable under section 80 is:

readLink.label: Read: Interest where no rate is specified, s. 80 →

options.explanation: This runs the statutory 18 per cent for a full year. The period from the due date to payment is eight months, not twelve.
This halves the statutory rate to 9 per cent. Section 80 fixes 18 per cent per annum and leaves no discretion in the parties.
Correct. Where no rate is specified, s. 80 supplies 18 per cent per annum running from the date the money OUGHT TO HAVE BEEN PAID: ₹ 4,50,000 × 18% × 8/12 = ₹ 54,000.

options.text: Nothing, because the instrument itself specifies no rate of interest
options.explanation: Silence is exactly the situation s. 80 addresses; it supplies the rate the parties omitted, notwithstanding any agreement between them about interest.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 98 · When notice of dishonour is unnecessary
questions.stem: In which of the following is notice of dishonour still NECESSARY?

readLink.label: Read: When notice of dishonour is unnecessary, s. 98 →

options.text: In order to charge the drawer, where he has countermanded payment
options.explanation: This is one of the eight cases in s. 98; a drawer who stopped the cheque already knows it will not be paid.

options.text: Where the party entitled to notice, knowing the facts, has promised unconditionally to pay the amount due
options.explanation: This too is in s. 98; the unconditional promise makes the notice pointless.

options.text: Where the instrument was accepted for the accommodation of the party entitled to notice
options.explanation: This is also in s. 98, because the accommodating party never owed the money in the first place.

options.text: In order to charge an endorser who has taken no part in the transaction since endorsing the instrument
options.explanation: Correct. Section 35 makes an endorser liable only where due notice of dishonour has been given to or received by him, and nothing in the s. 98 list excuses notice merely because he has been inactive.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 99, 100, 104 · Noting and protest
questions.stem: Which statement about noting and protest is correct?

readLink.label: Read: Noting and protest →

options.text: Protest of an inland instrument is optional, while a foreign bill must be protested where the law of the place where it was drawn requires it
options.explanation: Correct. Section 103 leaves protest of an inland bill or note to the holder's option, and s. 104 makes protest compulsory for a foreign bill in the circumstances the law of the place of drawing prescribes.

options.text: Noting must be done by the holder himself and protest by the drawer
options.explanation: Both are acts of a NOTARY PUBLIC, done at the instance of the holder; neither is performed by the drawer.

options.text: Protest may be made only where the instrument has been dishonoured by non-payment
options.explanation: Section 100 also covers dishonour by non-acceptance, and it provides separately for protest for better security where the acceptor becomes insolvent before maturity.

options.text: A formal protest must be drawn up in full within the time allowed, or the right to protest is lost
options.explanation: Section 104A says the opposite: it is enough that the instrument has been NOTED for protest in time, and the formal protest may be extended afterwards during the notary's business hours.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 87 · Material alteration
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a material alteration of a negotiable instrument?

readLink.label: Read: The effect of a material alteration, s. 87 →

options.text: Altering the date of the instrument
options.explanation: The date fixes maturity and therefore the whole timetable of the instrument; altering it is material.

options.text: Altering the sum payable
options.explanation: The sum is the core of the obligation and its alteration is the plainest example of a material alteration.

options.text: Converting an endorsement in blank into an endorsement in full
options.explanation: Correct. Section 49 expressly authorises a holder to do this, so it is not a material alteration; the same is true of filling in the blanks of an inchoate instrument under s. 20 and of crossing a cheque in the ways s. 125 permits.

options.text: Adding a place of payment where none was stated
options.explanation: Adding a place of payment changes where presentment must be made and is treated as material.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 31 · Liability of the drawee of a cheque
questions.stem: Ashraf's bank wrongly returns his cheque unpaid although his account held ample funds properly applicable to it. The payee's business relationship with Ashraf is damaged and Ashraf's own credit suffers. Under section 31:

readLink.label: Read: Liability of the drawee of a cheque, s. 31 →

options.text: The payee may sue the bank, because the cheque was an order addressed to it
options.explanation: The payee has no contract with the bank and the bank owes him no duty on the cheque; his remedy is against the drawer.

options.text: The drawer and the payee may sue the bank jointly for the loss each has suffered
options.explanation: Section 31 names a single beneficiary of the duty. The payee has no claim to join.

options.text: Neither may sue, because a banker has an absolute discretion whether to pay a cheque
options.explanation: There is no such discretion where the funds are sufficient and properly applicable; the section imposes a duty to pay.

options.text: Only Ashraf, the drawer, may sue the bank for the loss or damage caused by the wrongful dishonour
options.explanation: Correct. Section 31 makes the drawee bank answerable to its own customer, the drawer, for the damage to his credit, and to nobody else on the instrument.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 54, 85, 128, 131 · Case: the cheque taken from the courier bag
questions.case: Sandhya Enterprises draws a cheque for ₹ 3,60,000 on Kaveri Bank, payable to 'Hemanth Steels or order', and crosses it with two parallel transverse lines and nothing else. Hemanth Steels endorses the cheque in blank and sends it by courier to its supplier, Iqbal Metals. The envelope is opened in transit by a courier employee, who takes the cheque and pays it into his own small savings account with Malabar Bank, saying it came to him in settlement of a private loan. Malabar Bank makes no enquiry at all about how the holder of a modest salary account came by a cheque for ₹ 3,60,000, and collects the proceeds for him. Kaveri Bank pays the cheque to Malabar Bank in the ordinary clearing, the endorsement appearing regular on its face. Iqbal Metals never receives the cheque.

readLink.label: Read: Crossing of cheques →

questions.stem: The effect of Hemanth Steels endorsing the cheque in blank was that:
questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 16, 54 · Blank endorsement

options.text: The cheque became payable to bearer and thereafter passed by delivery alone
options.explanation: Correct. An endorsement in blank is the endorser's signature only (s. 16), and s. 54 makes an instrument so endorsed payable to bearer thereafter, which is exactly why a blank-endorsed cheque is as dangerous to lose as cash.

options.text: The cheque remained payable to order and could pass only on a further endorsement by Iqbal Metals
options.explanation: That would be the position after a FULL endorsement naming Iqbal Metals. A blank endorsement names nobody.

options.text: The cheque ceased to be negotiable, the payee having parted with it
options.explanation: Endorsing an instrument is the ordinary way of negotiating it; nothing about a blank endorsement destroys negotiability.

options.text: The general crossing was cancelled, because a blank endorsement overrides a crossing
options.explanation: An endorsement and a crossing operate on different things. The crossing survives untouched and still binds the paying banker under s. 126.

questions.stem: The position of Kaveri Bank, the paying banker, is that it:
questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 85, 126, 128 · Paying banker

options.text: Is liable to Hemanth Steels, because it paid a cheque that had been stolen
options.explanation: A paying banker is not an insurer against theft. Its duty is to observe the crossing and to pay in due course, both of which it did.

options.text: Is protected, having observed the crossing by paying a banker and having paid in due course on an endorsement regular on its face
options.explanation: Correct. Section 126 was observed because payment went to a banker; s. 128 then places the paying banker in the same position as if the amount had been paid to the true owner, and s. 85 protects payment in due course where the endorsement appears regular.

options.text: Is liable under s. 129, because a generally crossed cheque may be paid only to the named payee
options.explanation: Section 129 bites only where a crossed cheque is paid OTHERWISE than to a banker. A general crossing directs payment to a banker, not to the payee personally.

options.text: Is protected only if it can show that it verified the identity of the person who ultimately received the money
options.explanation: The paying banker deals with the collecting banker, not with the ultimate recipient; identifying him is the collecting banker's task.

questions.stem: The position of Malabar Bank, the collecting banker, is that it:
questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 131 · Collecting banker

options.text: Is protected by s. 131, because it collected the cheque for a customer
options.explanation: Collecting for a customer is only the first condition. Section 131 also requires good faith AND absence of negligence.

options.text: Is protected, because the cheque had become a bearer instrument and needed no enquiry
options.explanation: A bearer instrument still leaves the collecting banker with a duty to enquire where the circumstances are suspicious; the form of the instrument does not excuse negligence.

options.text: Loses the s. 131 protection and is liable to Hemanth Steels as true owner, because it made no enquiry in plainly suspicious circumstances
options.explanation: Correct. Section 131 protects only a banker who receives payment for a customer in good faith AND WITHOUT NEGLIGENCE; collecting a ₹ 3,60,000 cheque into a small savings account without a single question is the standard example of negligence, and the true owner is Hemanth Steels because the negotiation to Iqbal Metals was never completed by delivery.

options.text: Is liable to Sandhya Enterprises, the drawer, for the whole amount
options.explanation: The drawer's account was properly debited and it has lost nothing; the claim belongs to the true owner of the cheque.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 92 to 100, 119 · Case: the Nagpur bill that came back unpaid
questions.case: Vaibhavi Exports of Nagpur draws a bill on Tanmay Traders, also of Nagpur, for ₹ 5,40,000, payable three months after date. Tanmay accepts the bill. Vaibhavi endorses it to Prerna Mills, which endorses it to Quresh Brothers, the present holder. All four are in Nagpur. On the due date Quresh Brothers duly present the bill to Tanmay Traders for payment and Tanmay refuses to pay. Quresh Brothers wish to hold both Vaibhavi Exports and Prerna Mills liable on the bill, and also want the dishonour recorded so that they do not have to prove presentment and refusal if the matter reaches a Court years later. The bill is an inland bill.

readLink.label: Read: Dishonour and notice of dishonour →

questions.stem: To hold BOTH Vaibhavi Exports and Prerna Mills severally liable, Quresh Brothers must:
questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 93, 95 · Who gives notice, and to whom

options.text: Give notice of dishonour to each of them, since notice must go to every party whom the holder seeks to make severally liable
options.explanation: Correct. Section 93 requires the holder to give notice to ALL other parties whom he seeks to make severally liable, and to only one of several parties whom he seeks to make jointly liable.

options.text: Give notice only to Prerna Mills, his immediate endorser, who must then pass it back up the chain
options.explanation: Section 95 does oblige a party receiving notice to transmit it, but a holder who wants to sue a remoter party himself must give that party notice under s. 93.

options.text: Give notice only to Tanmay Traders, the party in default
options.explanation: Notice goes to the parties the holder wants to make liable, not to the acceptor who has already refused and plainly knows of the dishonour.

options.text: File a suit within thirty days, notice of dishonour being unnecessary on an accepted bill
options.explanation: Nothing in s. 98 excuses notice merely because the bill was accepted, and the thirty-day period belongs to s. 138, which applies only to cheques.

questions.stem: All the parties being at Nagpur, the notice of dishonour is given in due time if it is:
questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 94 · Time and mode of notice

options.text: Given orally at any time before the holder files his suit
options.explanation: The notice may indeed be oral, but it must go out within a reasonable time after the dishonour, not at any time before suit.

options.text: Despatched in time to reach its destination on the day next after the day of dishonour
options.explanation: Correct. Where the parties carry on business or live in the same place, s. 94 treats the notice as given in due time if it is despatched in time to reach the addressee on the day next after the day of dishonour.

options.text: Sent by registered post within thirty days of the dishonour
options.explanation: The Act prescribes no thirty-day period for notice of dishonour and no particular mode of despatch; the thirty days belong to proviso (b) to s. 138.

options.text: Given in writing only, an oral notice being ineffective under the Act
options.explanation: Section 94 expressly allows a notice of dishonour to be oral or written; writing is required only for the demand notice under s. 138.

questions.stem: On the wish to have the dishonour formally recorded, the correct advice is that:
questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 99, 100, 103, 119 · Noting and protest

options.text: Noting and protest are compulsory for this bill, and the holder loses his remedy if he omits them
options.explanation: Section 103 leaves protest of an inland bill to the holder's option; only a foreign bill may be compelled to be protested, and then only where the law of the place of drawing requires it.

options.text: Noting and protest are pointless once notice of dishonour has been given
options.explanation: They serve a different purpose. Notice preserves the claim; noting and protest preserve the EVIDENCE of the dishonour.

options.text: They are optional for an inland bill, but a protest is worth obtaining because s. 119 lets the Court presume the fact of dishonour on proof of it
options.explanation: Correct. Section 103 makes protest optional here, while s. 119 gives the holder who obtained one a real advantage at the trial: the dishonour is presumed unless and until it is disproved.

options.text: Only a formal protest drawn up on the day of dishonour will serve; a noting made that day is of no use
options.explanation: Section 104A provides that noting in time is enough, and the formal protest may be extended afterwards during the notary's business hours.

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 138 to 142 · Case: the dishonoured cheque of Rithika Polymers
questions.case: Rithika Polymers Private Limited owes Nandana Packaging ₹ 9,50,000 for a supply of cartons. Sameer, its managing director, signs a company cheque for that sum on Godavari Bank, dated 12 May 2026, and gives it to Nandana Packaging. Nandana banks the cheque on 24 June 2026 and it is returned unpaid, marked 'funds insufficient'. Nandana's bank hands Nandana the return memo on 27 June 2026. Nandana promptly posts a written demand for the cheque amount, and the demand is received by Rithika Polymers on 6 July 2026. Rithika pays nothing. Throughout, count a period expressed in days from and excluding the trigger date, and a period expressed in months to the corresponding date of the later month.

readLink.label: Read: Dishonour of a cheque, s. 138 →

questions.stem: Before s. 138 can operate at all on these facts, the requirement in the first proviso that must be satisfied is that:
questions.topic: Ch 7 · s. 138 proviso (a) · Presentment within validity

options.text: The cheque was presented to the bank within its period of validity, which is three months from the date it bears
options.explanation: Correct. Proviso (a) is the gateway: the cheque dated 12 May 2026 could be presented up to 12 August 2026, and presentment on 24 June 2026 is comfortably inside that window.

options.text: Notice of dishonour under s. 93 was given to the drawer within a reasonable time
options.explanation: Section 93 preserves the CIVIL claim on an instrument. It is not one of the three provisos to s. 138 and has no part in the criminal machinery.

options.text: The cheque was returned unpaid for any reason whatever
options.explanation: The section is confined to a return for insufficiency of funds or because the amount exceeds the arrangement with the bank; a purely technical return such as a signature mismatch is outside it.

options.text: The drawer knew, when he issued the cheque, that it would be dishonoured
options.explanation: Section 140 shuts out the opposite argument, that the drawer had no reason to believe the cheque would bounce; his state of mind is irrelevant either way.
