questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 4, 5, 6 · The three instruments
questions.stem: Define a promissory note, a bill of exchange and a cheque under the Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, and distinguish between them. (6 marks)

readLink.label: Read: Promissory note, bill of exchange and cheque →

skeleton.point: Promissory note: an instrument in writing, not being a bank note or currency note, containing an unconditional undertaking signed by the maker to pay a certain sum of money only to, or to the order of, a certain person or to the bearer

Bill of exchange: an instrument in writing containing an unconditional order, signed by the maker, directing a certain person to pay a certain sum of money only to, or to the order of, a certain person or to the bearer

Cheque: a bill of exchange drawn on a specified banker and not expressed to be payable otherwise than on demand, including the electronic image of a truncated cheque and a cheque in the electronic form

Nature and parties: a note is a promise made by the debtor with two parties (maker and payee); a bill is an order given by the creditor with three parties (drawer, drawee and payee); a cheque is a species of bill whose drawee can only be a banker

Acceptance and grace: a note is never accepted and a cheque needs no acceptance, while a time bill must be accepted before the drawee is liable; a time note and a time bill get three days of grace, and a cheque, being payable on demand, gets none

Other differences: notes and bills require a stamp while a cheque does not; only a cheque may be crossed; the maker of a note and the acceptor of a bill are primarily liable, while on a cheque the drawer is

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 8, 9 · Holder and holder in due course
questions.stem: Distinguish between a 'holder' and a 'holder in due course', and state the privileges which the Act confers on a holder in due course. (6 marks)

readLink.label: Read: Holder and holder in due course →

skeleton.point: Holder: a person entitled in his own name to the possession of the instrument and to receive or recover the amount due on it from the parties to it; where the instrument is lost or destroyed, the person so entitled at the time of the loss

Holder in due course: a person who, FOR CONSIDERATION, became the possessor (if payable to bearer) or the payee or endorsee (if payable to order) BEFORE the amount became payable, and WITHOUT sufficient cause to believe that any defect existed in the title of the person from whom he derived his title

Distinction: consideration and acquisition before maturity are essential for a holder in due course but not for a holder; a holder in due course takes free of the defects in his transferor's title, while a holder takes no better title than his transferor had; every holder in due course is a holder, but not the converse

Privileges (first group): an inchoate stamped instrument may be enforced for the whole amount filled in within the stamp (s. 20); every prior party is liable until the instrument is duly satisfied (s. 36); the acceptor of a bill drawn in a fictitious name is not relieved from liability (s. 42)

Privileges (second group): want of consideration is no defence (s. 43); conditional or special-purpose delivery is no defence (ss. 46, 47); a holder deriving title from a holder in due course takes the same clean title (s. 53); an instrument obtained by an offence, fraud or unlawful consideration is still enforceable by him (s. 58)

Privileges (estoppels): the maker, drawer and acceptor for honour cannot deny the validity of the instrument as originally made or drawn (s. 120); the maker and the acceptor of a bill payable to order cannot deny the payee's capacity to endorse (s. 121); an endorser cannot deny the signature or capacity of any prior party (s. 122)

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 16, 50, 52, 56 · Kinds of endorsement
questions.stem: Explain the different kinds of endorsement recognised by the Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, indicating the effect of each. (5 marks)

readLink.label: Read: The kinds of endorsement →

skeleton.point: Meaning: an endorsement is the signing of an instrument, otherwise than as maker, for the purpose of negotiation, on the back or face or on an annexed slip (an allonge); the signer is the endorser and the person to whom it passes is the endorsee
Blank or general endorsement: the endorser signs his name only, and the instrument becomes payable to bearer and passes thereafter by delivery alone
Full or special endorsement: the endorser adds a direction to pay to, or to the order of, a specified person, who becomes the endorsee; the instrument remains payable to order
Restrictive endorsement: express words restrict or exclude the right of further negotiation, or constitute the endorsee a mere agent to endorse or to receive the contents for the endorser

Endorsement sans recours and conditional endorsement: the endorser may exclude his own liability, or make it depend on a specified event; where he excludes his liability and later becomes the holder, all intermediate endorsers are liable to him

Partial endorsement: a writing purporting to transfer only part of the amount due is invalid for the purpose of negotiation, but where the amount has been partly paid a note of that fact may be endorsed and the instrument negotiated for the residue; mention also sans frais and facultative endorsements

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 123 to 131A · Crossing of cheques
questions.stem: What is meant by the crossing of a cheque? Explain the kinds of crossing and the legal effect of each, and state the protection the Act gives to the paying and the collecting banker. (6 marks)

readLink.label: Read: Crossing of cheques →

skeleton.point: Meaning: a crossing is a direction to the paying banker not to pay the cheque over the counter but only to a banker, so that the money passes through an account and leaves a trail; crossing applies only to cheques

General crossing: two parallel transverse lines across the face, with or without the words 'and company' or an abbreviation, and with or without the words 'not negotiable'; the drawee must not pay it otherwise than to a banker

Special crossing: the addition of the name of a banker, with or without the words 'not negotiable'; the lines are not essential, and the drawee must not pay otherwise than to that banker or his agent for collection. Under s. 127 a cheque crossed specially to more than one banker must be refused payment unless the second is a collecting agent

Who may cross and when: the holder may cross an uncrossed cheque, may make a general crossing special, and may add the words 'not negotiable'; a banker to whom a cheque is crossed specially may cross it again to his collecting agent. A crossing may only be made more restrictive

'Not negotiable' crossing: the cheque remains transferable, but a person taking it cannot have, and cannot give, a better title than the person from whom he took it had. 'Account payee' is not defined in the Act; it is banking practice and operates as a direction to the collecting banker

Protection: the paying banker who pays a crossed cheque in due course is placed in the position of one who paid the true owner (s. 128), and is protected on the endorsement by s. 85; payment out of due course makes him liable to the true owner (s. 129). The collecting banker who receives payment for a customer in good faith and without negligence is protected by s. 131, and s. 131A applies the crossing rules to bank drafts

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 21 to 25 · Maturity and the due date
questions.stem: State the rules laid down by the Negotiable Instruments Act 1881 for determining the date of maturity of a promissory note or bill of exchange, and illustrate them with an example. (5 marks)

readLink.label: Read: Maturity, days of grace and the due date →

skeleton.point: Meaning of maturity: the date at which the instrument falls due. 'At sight' and 'on presentment' mean on demand; 'after sight' means after acceptance (or noting or protest for non-acceptance) on a bill, and after presentment for sight on a promissory note

Days of grace: every note or bill not expressed to be payable on demand, at sight or on presentment is at maturity on the third day after the day on which it is expressed to be payable; an instrument payable on demand and a cheque get no grace

Months: the period terminates on the day of the month corresponding to the date, the sight or the event, and where the month has no corresponding day, on the last day of that month; months are never converted into thirty-day blocks
Days: the day of the date, of the presentment for acceptance or sight, of the protest for non-acceptance, or on which the event happens, is excluded from the count

Public holidays: where the day of maturity is a public holiday, including a Sunday or a day notified by the Central Government, the instrument is deemed due on the next PRECEDING business day; the days of grace are added before this test is applied, and by commercial practice an emergency holiday moves payment to the next succeeding business day

Illustration: a bill dated 30 November 2026 payable three months after date is expressed to be payable on 28 February 2027 (February having no 30th) and matures on 3 March 2027; a bill dated 29 June 2026 payable three months after date matures on 2 October 2026, and because that is a notified holiday it is due on 1 October 2026

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 91 to 98 · Dishonour and notice of dishonour
questions.stem: When is a negotiable instrument said to be dishonoured? Explain who must give notice of dishonour and to whom, and state the cases in which such notice is unnecessary. (6 marks)

readLink.label: Read: Dishonour and notice of dishonour →

skeleton.point: Dishonour by non-acceptance: where the drawee makes default in acceptance on being duly required to accept, where presentment is excused and the bill is not accepted, where the drawee is incompetent to contract, or where a qualified acceptance is treated by the holder as a dishonour

Dishonour by non-payment: where the maker, acceptor or drawee makes default in payment on being duly required to pay; where presentment for payment is unnecessary under s. 76, the instrument is dishonoured at the due date

Who gives notice and to whom: the holder, or any party who remains liable on the instrument, must give notice to all other parties whom he seeks to make severally liable, and to any one of several parties whom he seeks to make jointly liable

Mode and time: the notice may be oral or written, may be sent by post, and must convey that the instrument has been dishonoured and in what way and that the party will be held liable; it must be given within a reasonable time at the place of business or residence. Where the parties are in different places it is in time if posted the day after the dishonour; where they are in the same place it must be despatched to arrive the day after

When notice is unnecessary (first four): where it is dispensed with by the party entitled to it; to charge the drawer where he has countermanded payment; where the party charged could not suffer damage for want of notice; where the party entitled cannot after due search be found, or the party bound to give notice is unable without fault to give it

When notice is unnecessary (remaining four): to charge the drawers where the acceptor is also a drawer; where the promissory note is not negotiable; where the party entitled, knowing the facts, promises unconditionally to pay; and where the instrument was made or accepted for the accommodation of the party entitled to notice

questions.topic: Ch 7 · ss. 138 to 142 · Dishonour of a cheque for insufficiency of funds
questions.stem: State the ingredients of the offence under section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act 1881, the conditions in its three provisos, and the rules in sections 139 to 142 governing the presumption, the liability of a company and the taking of cognizance. (7 marks)

readLink.label: Read: Dishonour of a cheque, s. 138 →

skeleton.point: Ingredients: the cheque must be drawn by the accused on his own account with a banker, for the discharge in whole or in part of a legally enforceable debt or other liability, and must be returned unpaid because the funds in the account are insufficient or because the amount exceeds the arrangement made with the bank
Punishment: imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years, or a fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or both
Proviso (a): the cheque must have been presented to the bank within its period of validity, which by banking practice is three months from the date it bears

Proviso (b): the payee or holder in due course must make a demand for payment of the cheque amount by written notice to the drawer within thirty days of receiving information from the bank that the cheque has been returned unpaid
Proviso (c): the drawer must fail to make payment within fifteen days of receiving that notice; the offence is complete, and the cause of action arises, on the expiry of that fifteen-day period

Presumption and excluded defence: the Court shall presume, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder received the cheque for the discharge of a debt or other liability (s. 139); and it is no defence that the drawer had no reason to believe when he issued the cheque that it might be dishonoured (s. 140)

Offences by companies: the company and every person in charge of and responsible to it for the conduct of its business are deemed guilty, subject to a defence of want of knowledge or of due diligence; an officer with whose consent or connivance, or through whose neglect, the offence was committed is also liable. 'Company' includes a firm, and 'director' includes a partner

Cognizance: only on a written complaint by the payee or holder in due course, made within one month of the date on which the cause of action arises, though the Court may condone delay on sufficient cause; the case is triable by no Court inferior to a Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate of the first class, and jurisdiction follows the bank branch where the cheque was delivered for collection or presented. Every offence under the Act is compoundable under s. 147
